tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

## What is counted
- Grand Theft Auto VI releases on 19 November 2026 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, single-player. No console maker publishes a player count, so the game has no public count of concurrent players. The count this contest forecasts is Twitch's own count of concurrent live viewers in the "Grand Theft Auto VI" category (Twitch game id 1867279146): the number of people watching its live streams at once, the figure Twitch's directory page shows for the category.
- The house reads it once a minute from Twitch's public GraphQL API (POST https://gql.twitch.tv/gql, Twitch's public web client id, the query game(id: "1867279146") { id name viewersCount broadcastersCount }), each read started at the minute's first second and tried up to 3 times inside the minute. A read is valid when Twitch answered for that game with a whole number of viewers and of channels (broadcastersCount, the live streams in the category), each 0 or more.
- An hour h of the release day (h = 1 to 24) runs from 2026-11-19T00:00:00Z + (h - 1) hours to the next whole hour, hour 1 from 00:00 to 01:00 UTC and hour 24 from 23:00 to 2026-11-20T00:00:00Z. The game unlocks at midnight local time, country by country (New Zealand first, at 2026-11-18T11:00:00Z; central Europe at 23:00 UTC; the UK at 00:00 UTC; the US east coast at 05:00 UTC and the west coast at 08:00 UTC), so the UTC day holds the unlock in most of the world.
- An hour's count (its print) is the mean of the viewers of the valid reads whose minute lies in that hour, rounded half up to a whole number of viewers, when the hour has at least 30 valid reads of its 60. An hour with fewer has no print and is not scored.

## The case
- The final has one case, h00, cut at the deadline, 2026-11-19T01:00:00Z, the end of hour 1: every valid read the house recorded before it and hour 1's print. If hour 1 has fewer than 30 valid reads, its print is the mean of the valid reads it has; with none there is no answer (The answer and the recording). The house records the reads while they happen, so no one, the house included, has the answer before the hours have passed.
- The practice is the same shape over four past big game launches, cases p00 to p03: Marvel's Wolverine (2026-09-15), Red Dead Redemption 2 (2018-10-26), God of War Ragnarök (2022-11-09) and Marvel's Spider-Man 2 (2023-10-20), all console games that unlocked at midnight local time. Each case's day is the UTC day of that game's release date, its hour 1 the day's first hour, its history the points the historical source (SullyGnome.com's hourly Twitch category averages) has before the end of hour 1, and its answer the hourly counts of hours 2 to 24 from the same source. That source gives one average a whole hour, not 60 minute reads, so a practice hour's print is that one point: close to the final's minute mean, not the same measure. Its notes say when that game really unlocked. No case holds another case's answer: the comparables in a practice case leave out every practice launch.

## Your input
- /input/<id>.in, the one case your run is given (h00, or a practice case such as p00): UTF-8 JSON, one object (schema "makefun/twitch-ccu-case/v1"):
- `id`; `game` (`name` "Grand Theft Auto VI" and `twitch_id` "1867279146" in the final, the launch's own in a practice case); `day_start` (the day's first instant, ISO 8601 UTC) and `checkpoint` (the end of hour 1); `levels` ([0.05,0.25,0.5,0.75,0.95]);
- `known`: hour 1's print, one row {`hour`: 1, `from`, `until`, `viewers`, `channels`, `reads`}; `forecast`: the 23 rows to forecast, {`hour`, `from`, `until`} for hours 2 to 24;

## Scoring
- Every case, each of its printed hours h from 2 to 24 and each of the five levels tau is one item. Its pinball loss is 2 x max(tau x d, (tau - 1) x d), where d = ln(y) - ln(q), y is the hour's print and q your quantile at tau for it: a quantile below the count costs 2 x tau per unit of log it is short, one above it 2 x (1 - tau) per unit it is over, so the 5% quantile should sit where the count is below it one hour in twenty. The log scale makes a miss of 20% cost the same at 10,000 viewers as at 1,000,000. A print below 1 viewer counts as 1 (the log of 0 is no number).
- Loss (the rank): the mean pinball loss over every item of every case, written to 6 decimals; lower is better and 0 is the best. A forecast whose five quantiles are equal scores exactly its mean absolute log error, the mean of |ln(y) - ln(q)|, so the most accurate forecast and an honest spread are scored on one scale. The board ranks on those 6 decimals; its public rows round it to 3 significant figures, and your own entries' rows, the result document and the archive keep it exact. Every rank, tie and prize is decided on the exact value.
- The board also shows the typical miss (100 x (exp(m) - 1), in percent, where m is the mean over every scored hour of |ln(y) - ln(your median)|), the 90% coverage (the share of scored hours with your 5% quantile at or below the print and your 95% quantile at or above it; an honest forecast covers about 0.9) and valid (1 when every case is valid, else 0). They are information: only the loss ranks.
- A worked example: say a case scores two hours and the forecast's rows for them are both [600000, 800000, 900000, 1100000, 1500000]. The first hour's print is 1,000,000: the five items cost 0.051083, 0.111572, 0.105361, 0.047655 and 0.040547. The second's is 700,000: 0.015415, 0.200297, 0.251314, 0.225993 and 0.076214. The loss is the mean of the ten, 0.112545; the typical miss 19.52%; the 90% coverage 1 (both prints inside the 5% to 95% band). Had that case been invalid with an hour-1 print of 1,200,000, every quantile would be 1,200,000 and its loss the mean absolute log error, (0.182322 + 0.538997) / 2 = 0.360659.
- Exactly equal losses are ordered by the run time, faster first: the grader's own measurement of the wall time your program takes over all of a phase's cases, averaged over its two executions, in whole milliseconds (run_ms), on the same 1-CPU sandbox every entry runs in; exactly equal run times go to the earlier receipt. It only breaks an exact tie and is never part of the loss.
- The pinball loss is a proper scoring rule for quantiles: you score best on average by writing the quantiles you really believe. A forecast that is too narrow pays for every hour outside it, one too wide pays at every hour, and one whose median sits where the count is not pays at both.

- Loss (the rank): the mean pinball loss over every item of every case, written to 6 decimals; lower is better and 0 is the best. A forecast whose five quantiles are equal scores exactly its mean absolute log error, the mean of |ln(y) - ln(q)|, so the most accurate forecast and an honest spread are scored on one scale. The board ranks on those 6 decimals; its public rows round it to 3 significant figures, and your own entries' rows, the result document and the archive keep it exact. Every rank, tie and prize is decided on the exact value.

It reads the category once a minute from before the opening until 2026-11-20T00:10:00Z, in two places, a primary and a backup: for each minute the primary's read counts, and a minute the primary missed is filled from the backup's.
41	- An hour with fewer than 30 valid reads has no print and is not scored. The final needs at least 12 of the 23 hours printed: with fewer, or with no valid read in hour 1, there is no answer, the final is not graded and no prize is paid (Payout).
42	- Once the day is recorded, the house freezes the recording into the final dataset, which is attached to the final phase and published with the results: the case every entry read and every print, so anyone can score every final entry again on the same counts.
43	- Before the deadline the practice cases are scored the same way against the historical source's counts. The practice is graded on past launches anyone can look up and pays nothing, so a practice score is no guide to the final.
44	
45	## The race
46	- After the deadline the final runs as a race you can watch. At the deadline the house runs every racing entry once on h00, cut from the live recording, and keeps its forecast; then at the end of each hour from 2026-11-19T02:00:00Z to 2026-11-20T00:00:00Z it scores the hour just ended against that hour's print, with the loss above, and the race's chart and standings show each racer's loss over the hours scored so far.
47	- Up to 256 final entries race, seated by their practice rank, the house entries among them. The race's marks are provisional and decide nothing: the result is the official grade of every final entry on the frozen recording, the same prints, once the final phase grades it.
48	
49	## Baseline and prizes
50	- The house baseline (starter/main.ts in the kit) says every hour stays at the first hour's count, with a spread that widens over the day: for hour h = 2 to 24, q_tau = p x exp(z_tau x 0.15 x sqrt(h - 1)), rounded to 2 decimals, where p is hour 1's print (1 if it is below 1) and z_tau the standard normal's quantile at each level (-1.645, -0.674, 0, 0.674, 1.645). After a first hour of 100,000 viewers its hour-2 row runs from 78,133.6 to 127,985.91 around 100,000, and its hour-24 row from 30,624.45 to 326,536.46. Its numbers were fixed in advance, never tuned on the practice. On the practice it scores a loss of about 0.387 (typical miss about 82.8%, 90% coverage about 0.783, every case valid); the kit's starter, the same program, scores the same. It is graded on the final like every entry.
51	- The house model forecast: the house also enters the forecast of an AI model (superbot, at reasoning effort max, with a 64,000-token output budget), made by one recorded call the house pays for (asked once more, the same prompt, only if its first answer is not a valid forecast), given these rules, the forecast's format and the case's data. It answers, for each case and each of hours 2 to 24, a median ratio r_h to the case's hour-1 print and a log spread s_h. Its answer is recorded, and every grading replays it with no new call: q_tau = p x r_h x exp(z_tau x s_h), p the case's hour-1 print. It is made once for the practice, over the practice cases, and once for the final, at 2026-11-18T23:00:00Z, two hours before the deadline, on the history recorded to then, before hour 1 has begun: its ratios are to hour 1's print, whatever it turns out to be, and they are replayed on h00.
52	- Twenty places pay $250 in USDC: $50 for 1st place, $35 for 2nd, $25 for 3rd, $10 each for 4th to 10th and $7 each for 11th to 20th, one place per entrant. Places go by loss, lowest first, so 1st place is the best forecast that beats the best house entry. Beating the best house entry makes a forecast eligible, not a winner: when more than twenty forecasts beat it, only the twenty with the lowest losses take places. A prize needs a loss strictly below the best house entry's on the final: the house baseline's or the house model forecast's, whichever is lower (the house baseline's alone if the house model forecast was not entered), and every case valid. An entry at or above it keeps its rank but takes no place, and the next entry below it takes the place. The house baseline and the house model forecast rank on the leaderboard and take no place, since the bar is the lower of their losses and neither is below it; any other entry make.fun enters itself ranks like any other entry and must beat them too. A house bot that finishes in a paid place holds that place, and that place's prize is not awarded; no entry moves up to take it. A place no entry is left to take is not awarded. Exactly equal losses go to the faster program, then the earlier receipt.
53	
54	## Transcripts
55	Every submission must include the transcripts of the AI coding-agent sessions that built it (the session logs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or another agent harness writes while it runs), as a makefun bundle or as loose files, up to 200 MB. A session file exported afterwards (a SpecStory export, or a chat log your agent writes out) must carry the model provider's usage on its assistant messages and name the harness that wrote it; one your agent hands over because its tool keeps no session record (a session file it exported itself carrying "handed_over") need not carry usage, and its entry is ranked but takes no paid place; a ChatGPT or Claude account export carries no usage and is not accepted. Secrets are redacted on the server. The transcripts are matched against the code for authorship and priced for build cost. Code written by hand is allowed; it lowers authored coverage.
56	
57	## Transcript gate
58	Before an entry is graded, its transcripts pass a gate of ten pass/fail checks. The gate is never a score, and it has no AI judge and no AI-text detection: no check reads what a thinking block says, so a session whose thinking the provider summarised or left out passes on what the agent did. An entry that fails any check is rejected: it is not graded and takes no prize, and its status names each failed check with its fix, so you can fix it and submit again before the deadline.
59	- transcripts_present: at least one session is parsed from the upload.
60	- transcripts_recorded: every session is a log a harness recorded or a file exported from its record; a session your agent hands over because its tool keeps no session record (a session file it exported itself carrying "handed_over", one line saying why) makes this check skip as a note naming it, never a rejection, and the entry's build cost is labelled Handed over; under handed_over_places none: An entry with a handed-over session is ranked where it scores but takes no paid place: to compete for rewards, tell the person you work for to run you in a client whose sessions are recorded. If you cannot hand over what you can see, use Superbot (https://superbot.gg), a free client: run on your own computer, it keeps sessions that bundle reads.
61	- thinking_wellformed: every user, assistant and tool message of a session carries a timestamp (a handed-over session's messages may carry none, and the times they carry are held to the rest), no assistant or tool message falls more than 60 s behind the latest before it, and every tool result answers one earlier tool call of its session; a session file your agent exported itself names the harness that wrote it, in the file or with bundle's --harness.
62	- thinking_in_window: every transcript timestamp lies between the competition's opening and the entry's receipt time, give or take 60 s of clock skew.
63	- thinking_reproduces: at least 30% of the counted lines are authored, first carried by a write or edit of the agent's own in the transcripts; a line that first appears in a human's message (pasted), in a tool result or a file read back (read) or nowhere in them (absent), and a line the agent re-typed, renamed or reformatted from code a tool result or a message showed it first (copied: code cloned, downloaded, copied or pasted in), count against the share, and the lines of the kit's starter, as handed out or re-typed from it, are left out of the counted lines; at most 40% of the counted lines of text files are unwritten: absent, or read in a file an import command the agent ran brought in (git clone, curl or wget to a file, cp from outside the repository, an archive unpacked, a project generator), which fails only once 10 or more lines are; and the entrypoint (main.ts or main.py) has at least one authored line; a packed entrypoint the kit's makefun compress wrote counts as the source it was packed from, which bundle uploads beside the sessions, when makefun compress makes the entrypoint from that source byte for byte and the sessions show the agent writing the source and then running makefun compress on it later than the latest message in which one of the source's authored lines first appears (an edit that only deletes or re-types lines is no write), shown by the agent's own command running makefun compress on the source or by the line makefun compress prints, in a tool result or any other message; the source's lines then count toward the share as any counted file's do, a line repeated in it counted once.
64	- thinking_turns: at least 5 assistant turns carry text or thinking (a turn that only calls tools does not count).
65	- thinking_priced: every usage record prices to a known model, or to $0 where the record's session ran its model on your own machine (a local runtime or loopback server the session records, never a model's name or a self-export's stated provider), for this check alone, never the entry's build cost; a self-reported session (a file exported afterwards, not a log a known harness wrote; a file in Claude Code's or Muse Code's session format without the token usage those harnesses record on every response, or in Claude Code's without its version, is one) carries the provider's usage on at least 50% of its assistant messages, with the provider's own token counts, not rounded, estimated or repeated figures (a provider's input count grows as the conversation does, so one pair of counts does not keep coming back), and its output is no more than a model produces in the time its own timestamps span (500 tokens a second); a handed-over session need not carry usage, but the usage it does carry is held to the same rules; an upload of harness-recorded logs with no usage has nothing to price; an entry whose sessions are the Muse app's own session files carries its agent's token usage as Muse recorded it (at least one usage row across them), attached with bundle's --muse-usage.
66	- thinking_revised: some file (the entrypoint, or the code it runs) takes its final content from at least 2 assistant messages that write or edit it (a file written once in full and never revised counts 1).
67	- thinking_fresh: for an entry uploaded as a source bundle, every credited line comes from agent sessions that show the anchor line the kit's init prints (makefun anchor <root sha> round <round>) in a tool result before their first counted write (a Claude subagent launched after its parent's quote, or a Codex fork of a session that quoted it, counts with it); short of that the check skips as a note: the entry is not rejected, and its reward, if it places, is paid as any other. A quote timestamped before the round fails.
68	- transcripts_run_record: an entry received from 17 November 2026 (00:00 UTC) carries a run record (bundle writes it into the bundle; a loose upload adds makefun-run.json) and is rejected without one, or with one its upload contradicts: its prompt is the person's own opening prompt, never blank, a template left unfilled or an agent's or a harness's hand-off, and one marked typed is the first message of an uploaded top-level session, while any other names what started the run; the harness, its version, the provider, the model and the effort are each declared or recorded by every top-level session (a model id that names its provider, such as claude-*, gives the provider; --effort default names the harness's own effort, and --effort none a real level); a system prompt marked uploaded comes as a system-prompt file, one marked in-session is carried by a session, and one withheld says why; every MCP server a session used (an mcp__<server>__<tool> tool it called, or a server its log lists) is listed by its name, and none is marked builtin unless a harness the sessions ran under ships it (Claude Code's ide, claude-in-chrome, workspace, computer-use, Claude Preview and Claude Browser, Claude Desktop's ccd_turn, Cosmos's cosmos and Codex's codex_apps); and the instruction files it states are collected only where the upload carries one, none only where it carries none, and withheld with a reason. An entry received before then with no run record skips as a note, and a run record it does carry is checked the same way.
69	
70	## Entries
71	- Node 22 (node /bot/main.ts) or Python 3.13 (python3 /bot/main.py): one of the two at the repository's root, not both. Source and the standard library only, nothing installed, no network.
72	- Your program is run once per case, each run in a sandbox of its own with only that case's file in /input: at most 8 seconds, 1 CPU, 1024 MB and 64 processes per run. /bot, your repository, is read-only; /output is where your forecast goes. Each phase's cases are run twice and the two forecasts of each case must be the same byte for byte, so seed any randomness. An entry whose two executions of any case differ is scored from the first and is not ranked.
73	- A practice grade runs your program twice on each practice case, each run starting a sandbox of its own: about 2 seconds a start when few entries are being graded, 8 to 11 seconds at full load (up to 20 at the 90th percentile), so on production a practice grade takes about 10 seconds a run when quiet and 15 to 20 seconds a run at full load, plus about 10 seconds.
74	- The kit's starter/ is the house baseline laid out as an entry, with an MIT LICENSE: run it locally on the practice with `mkdir -p out && MAKEFUN_INPUT_DIR=input MAKEFUN_OUTPUT_DIR=out node starter/main.ts` from the kit's directory (starter/main.py is the same program in Python).
75	- Entries are taken from the opening at 2026-11-17T06:00:00Z to the deadline at 2026-11-19T01:00:00Z. At most 10 submissions a day and 20 in all; your last submission before the deadline is your final entry. Every entry needs the transcripts of the agent sessions that built it.
76	- The entry signature: a wallet linked to your account signs the entry message (make.fun entry v1), which names this site, the competition, the repository, the commit, the sha256 of the transcripts uploaded with it, the wallet, a fresh nonce and the time it was issued. A signed message is good for 10 minutes and enters one submission only. When the reward is locked in make.fun's escrow program on Solana, every entry is signed by a Solana wallet linked to your account, and a prize the entry wins is claimed from the escrow to that wallet (see Payout). Otherwise the reward is paid from make.fun's reward wallet and an entry needs no signature: a prize is claimed with the payout details alone, and an entry may still carry the signature. This bounty's page says which.

78	- Your repository is public on GitHub from the moment you create it, so anyone can read your code and see which GitHub account owns it, even though this site shows it only to you and the organisers.
79	
80	## Payout
81	The final leaderboard is published within 7 days of the deadline, unless a check holds it: the results come once the release day has been recorded and graded. Once the final dataset the house froze from its recording is attached, every final entry is graded on it, the runs that would be paid are graded again and the entries are scanned for copies, and the results are published and resolved with no further admin step. The prizes are paid in USDC on Solana only (no bank wire), in one of two ways, and this bounty's page says which. When the bounty opens, its whole reward is locked in make.fun's escrow program on Solana if the escrow can be funded. When the reward is locked in the escrow, every entry is signed by a Solana wallet linked to the entrant's account (see Entries), and once the result is posted each winner claims the prize from the escrow to the wallet that signed the winning entry, the claim screened against the sanctions list; a prize that nobody wins or claims goes back to make.fun's reward wallet after the escrow's claim window.
82	
83	Otherwise the reward is paid from make.fun's reward wallet as follows, and an entry needs no signature. Once the results are resolved, each winner claims the prize within 7 days with the payout details: a Solana address to pay it to and the winner agreement. A legal name, the country of residence and a tax form (a W-9 for a US person, a W-8BEN for anyone else) are asked only when the winner's prizes from make.fun in the calendar year, this prize included, reach the $2,000 tax reporting threshold; below it, the claim asks for none of them. The claim is screened against the sanctions list, then the house pays it from make.fun's reward wallet in USDC on Solana: at once when the address is a wallet linked to the winner's account by signature and the automatic checks clear it, otherwise once the organisers have screened it. A prize not claimed within 7 days passes to the next entry in the standings. A prize that no entry takes or claims (a place no prize-eligible entry is left to take, or one passed down the standings until no eligible entry is left) is never paid out: its money stays in make.fun's reward wallet for later contests.
84	
85	If there is no answer (The answer and the recording), no result is posted and no prize is paid, whichever way the reward was to be paid: a reward locked in the escrow goes back to make.fun's reward wallet once the escrow's resolve window, 14 days after the final phase ends, has passed with no result posted.
86	
87	Every prize is paid gross, subject to statutory withholding; any tax due on it is the winner's own.
88	
89	Open to individuals 18 or older (or the age of majority where they live), except residents of comprehensively sanctioned countries, anyone on a sanctions list, and where prohibited by law.

91	## The command line
92	cli/makefun.mjs is the makefun command line in one file, everything it needs inlined: it runs on Node 22 or later with nothing to install. kit.json lists its sha256 and size, as it does every file's here. Run it from this directory:
93

95	
96	Its commands talk to https://make.fun, the site this kit was downloaded from (cli/site.json names it), with no --origin and no register needed for that. The origin is --origin, else $MAKEFUN_ORIGIN, else the one register stored in ~/.makefun/credentials (the site you last registered with), else https://make.fun. 101	This is a program/v1 competition: its scorer and reference data stay on the server, which grades every entry; input/ holds the input data the entry reads. kit.json lists the sha256 and size of every file here.

Forecast GTA VI's launch-day Twitch viewers hour by hour

## The task
Start your agent's session at or after the competition opens (2026-11-17T06:00:00Z) and build your entry in it: a session that began before the opening cannot be entered (thinking_in_window, below). Forecast how many people watch Grand Theft Auto VI live on Twitch in each hour of its release day, 2026-11-19 (UTC), after the first. Your program, `node /bot/main.ts` (Node 22) or `python3 /bot/main.py` (Python 3.13) at the root of your repository, is run once per case: it reads that case's file at /input, everything recorded up to the end of the day's first hour, that hour's count included, and writes one forecast file to /output: for each of hours 2 to 24, five quantiles of that hour's count. It runs in a sandbox with no network, so it cannot read Twitch: it forecasts. Your score is the mean pinball loss on the log scale over every scored hour and quantile (Scoring).

## What is counted
- Grand Theft Auto VI releases on 19 November 2026 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, single-player. No console maker publishes a player count, so the game has no public count of concurrent players. The count this contest forecasts is Twitch's own count of concurrent live viewers in the "Grand Theft Auto VI" category (Twitch game id 1867279146): the number of people watching its live streams at once, the figure Twitch's directory page shows for the category.
- The house reads it once a minute from Twitch's public GraphQL API (POST https://gql.twitch.tv/gql, Twitch's public web client id, the query game(id: "1867279146") { id name viewersCount broadcastersCount }), each read started at the minute's first second and tried up to 3 times inside the minute. A read is valid when Twitch answered for that game with a whole number of viewers and of channels (broadcastersCount, the live streams in the category), each 0 or more.
- An hour h of the release day (h = 1 to 24) runs from 2026-11-19T00:00:00Z + (h - 1) hours to the next whole hour, hour 1 from 00:00 to 01:00 UTC and hour 24 from 23:00 to 2026-11-20T00:00:00Z. The game unlocks at midnight local time, country by country (New Zealand first, at 2026-11-18T11:00:00Z; central Europe at 23:00 UTC; the UK at 00:00 UTC; the US east coast at 05:00 UTC and the west coast at 08:00 UTC), so the UTC day holds the unlock in most of the world.
- An hour's count (its print) is the mean of the viewers of the valid reads whose minute lies in that hour, rounded half up to a whole number of viewers, when the hour has at least 30 valid reads of its 60. An hour with fewer has no print and is not scored.

## The case
- The final has one case, h00, cut at the deadline, 2026-11-19T01:00:00Z, the end of hour 1: every valid read the house recorded before it and hour 1's print. If hour 1 has fewer than 30 valid reads, its print is the mean of the valid reads it has; with none there is no answer (The answer and the recording). The house records the reads while they happen, so no one, the house included, has the answer before the hours have passed.
- The practice is the same shape over four past big game launches, cases p00 to p03: Marvel's Wolverine (2026-09-15), Red Dead Redemption 2 (2018-10-26), God of War Ragnarök (2022-11-09) and Marvel's Spider-Man 2 (2023-10-20), all console games that unlocked at midnight local time. Each case's day is the UTC day of that game's release date, its hour 1 the day's first hour, its history the points the historical source (SullyGnome.com's hourly Twitch category averages) has before the end of hour 1, and its answer the hourly counts of hours 2 to 24 from the same source. That source gives one average a whole hour, not 60 minute reads, so a practice hour's print is that one point: close to the final's minute mean, not the same measure. Its notes say when that game really unlocked. No case holds another case's answer: the comparables in a practice case leave out every practice launch.

## Your input
- /input/<id>.in, the one case your run is given (h00, or a practice case such as p00): UTF-8 JSON, one object (schema "makefun/twitch-ccu-case/v1"):
- `id`; `game` (`name` "Grand Theft Auto VI" and `twitch_id` "1867279146" in the final, the launch's own in a practice case); `day_start` (the day's first instant, ISO 8601 UTC) and `checkpoint` (the end of hour 1); `levels` ([0.05,0.25,0.5,0.75,0.95]);
- `known`: hour 1's print, one row {`hour`: 1, `from`, `until`, `viewers`, `channels`, `reads`}; `forecast`: the 23 rows to forecast, {`hour`, `from`, `until`} for hours 2 to 24;
- `history`: every valid point before the checkpoint, oldest first, each {`at`, `viewers`, `channels`}: in the final the house's minute reads since its recorder started, on 2026-11-17; in a practice case the historical source's points, at its own spacing, `channels` null where it has none; `history_hourly`: the same as whole-hour means, each {`from`, `viewers`, `channels`, `reads`};
- `streams`: the category's top 20 live streams at the last valid read before the checkpoint, each {`login`, `viewers`, `language`, `started_at`} (null in the practice); `categories_hourly`: Twitch's top 20 categories once an hour, each {`from`, `top`: [{`name`, `viewers`, `channels`}]} (null in the practice);
- `comparables`: past big launches' hourly counts from 14 days before their release day to 3 days after it (SullyGnome.com's hourly averages), each {`name`, `day_start`, `unlock`, `platforms`, `source`, `hourly`: [{`from`, `viewers`, `channels`}]}: 38 in a practice case, which leaves out the four practice launches, and all 42 in the final; one of them, in every case, is the Grand Theft Auto VI category's own hourly history from its 2026-08-27 extended-look premiere to 2026-11-17; and `notes`, where the case's data comes from.
- /input/NOTICE.txt is beside the cases in the kit's input/: where the counts come from and how to fetch them again. Your program is run with only its case's file there, so read every `*.in` file you find, in name order, and write one output for each.
- Your program reads $MAKEFUN_INPUT_DIR when that is set, else /input/, and writes to $MAKEFUN_OUTPUT_DIR when that is set, else /output/: the grader's container leaves both unset, and a run on your machine sets both (Entries, below).

## Your forecast
